corrected_value.title: The acquisition of abstract words by young infants.

decisions.quote: While the study was not designed to test the difference between noun and verb acquisition, 6–9-month-olds did perform well on one of the two verb pairs ( hug - eat ), contrary to their poor performance on a broader set of non-nouns in a prior study ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2013 ). Whether infants’ apparent success on hug-eat represents random item variation, or a first fragile glimmer of infants’ understanding of these verbs, is unclear, particularly given infants’ failure to demonstrate understanding of kiss-drink here.
decisions.reason: The replicating study empirically re-tests findings from Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) (DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2013.02.011) in a new sample of 6–16-month-old infants using paired dynamic video stimuli: it explicitly repeats the hug-eat verb pair tested in Bergelson & Swingley (2013b), tests whether 6–9-month-olds' prior failure on non-nouns in that dynamic-video study was due to dynamic video presentation versus word class, and re-tests the non-linear comprehension boost around 13–14 months reported in both Bergelson & Swingley (2012) and (2013b). Both the Works Cited list and Crossref metadata verify the identity of Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) in Cognition 127(3), 391–397. The sole shipped original (input_row_index 391, Bergelson & Swingley, 2012, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1113380109) is a separate PNAS article testing concrete food and body-part nouns with static images, and sibling missing target_index 4 (Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012, DOI 10.1111/j.1532-7078.2011.00084.x) is a distinct Infancy study on body-part nouns; report equivalence does not apply. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work.

decisions.quote: This study confirms several patterns that have emerged in previous work ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ; Parise & Csibra, 2012 ; Tincoff & Jusczyk, 1999 , 2012 ). Namely, we find further evidence, with a new sample of infants and a new set of item pairs, that 6-9 month olds understand words. Not unexpectedly, this ability increases with age, but perhaps less expectedly the rate with which it increases is non-linear. This is the third study that finds evidence of a boost in performance around 13-14 months, independent of word type ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ). We find three possible explanations for this boost viable. First, this is around the time that infants begin talking ( Dale & Fenson, 1996 ), which may increase their metalinguistic awareness, or understanding of words as community-wide symbols in a way that boosts comprehension . Second, this is just before the time that infants begin to show basic syntactic knowledge, and this in turn may help them use the distribution of arguments in the sentence to listen more predictively ( Jin & Fisher, 2014 ). decisions.reason: The complete Parise/Csibra original was independently recovered and inspected. Its specific empirical diagnostic is a word-object congruency N400 response, interpreted as referential semantic understanding rather than mere audiovisual association, present for live maternal but not yoked unfamiliar speech. The current report positively acknowledges this evidence and jointly confirms the broader early-word-comprehension pattern. Its own paired-video looking test, including live parental naming, however does not test the congruent/incongruent semantic-violation response, referential-versus-associative distinction or maternal-versus-unfamiliar speaker claim. It explicitly defines its empirical retest as common-noun comprehension across a wider set of paired moving referents, already represented by Bergelson/Swingley2012 and the directly extended Tincoff/Jusczyk2012 common-noun comparison. No later report is declared an intervening replication of Parise merely from timing or citation. This exclusion rests on the actual original-specific semantic-violation finding and current selected behavioral claim, not on EEG versus gaze measurement alone or omission of one experimental arm. The affirmative collective Discussion wording and current live-parent protocol are preserved as contrary context; no N400 result or semantic-mechanism finding is inferred from ordinary looking preference.

decisions.location: Introduction (final paragraph, chunk 8, chars 6704-7586); see also Discussion (chunk 28)
decisions.quote:
The present research examined early comprehension of words that were instantiated as competing video stimuli. We presented 6–16-month-old infants with a broad set of common words, such as “dog” and “car” (see Table 1 ). The words we tested had some overlap with previous work, but only one pair of nouns (hand-feet) had been tested before with young infants, as either still images or video clips ( Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012 ). We also included two pairs of verbs, one of which was tested in Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) . Thus, this study set out to replicate the basic finding of previous work, i.e. that young infants understand common nouns, while also extending the range of the words tested, and their format of presentation. The present study also extends previous findings in its methods, utilizing a varied series of video stimuli over twelve trials.

decisions.reason: Although Discussion chunk 28 includes Tincoff & Jusczyk (1999, DOI 10.1111/1467-9280.00127) in the five-study group citation for the broad pattern that 6-9-month-olds understand words, the primary abstract (infant_originals_0106) and Introduction chunk 5 show that Tincoff & Jusczyk (1999) specifically tested 6-month-olds' comprehension of the proper names 'Mommy' and 'Daddy' using videos of the infant's own parents versus unfamiliar parents (demonstrating parent-specific attachment-figure recognition rather than generic category comprehension). The present study tests six yoked pairs of common nouns and verbs (bottle-car, dog-bear, drink-kiss, hand-feet, hug-eat, juice-ball; chunk 11) and no proper names or parent videos. Crucially, when defining the study's empirical overlap and replication design in Introduction chunk 8 and Materials chunk 11, the authors explicitly link the paired-video common-noun retest to the closer follow-up paper Tincoff & Jusczyk (2012) ('only one pair of nouns (hand-feet) had been tested before with young infants, as either still images or video clips (Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012)'), along with Bergelson & Swingley (2012, shipped row 391) and Bergelson & Swingley (2013b, target 1). Thus, the empirical retest in the Tincoff & Jusczyk paired-video lineage is captured by the closer 2012 common-noun study (target 4) and shipped row 391, not the 1999 Mommy/Daddy study.
